description.value: The study examined whether individual differences in trait anxiety were associated with anticipatory somatosensory cortex activity during fear conditioning and investigated multisensory relationships among auditory cortex, amygdala, and somatosensory cortex.

design.value: Twenty healthy participants completed a one-run fear-conditioning task during fMRI. One of two tones was counterbalanced across participants as the CS+ and paired with electric shock on 50% of CS+ trials; the other tone was the CS−. Analyses examined condition differences, individual differences in trait anxiety, mediation among auditory cortex, amygdala, and right S1 activity, and condition-dependent functional connectivity.

description.value: An established measure of individual differences in anxiety, providing state anxiety (STAI-S) and trait anxiety (STAI-T) scores.

assessment_type.value: measure of individual differences in anxiety

description.value: Fear contingent responding was assessed using skin conductance response. Peak SCR amplitude from baseline was taken between 1–8 s after tone onset on a trial-by-trial basis and averaged as a function of CS tone.
Participants indicated by button press with their index or middle finger of the right hand whether the tone was low or high pitched immediately after hearing the tone.

source_definition.value: The first two critical regressors were for non-reinforced CS+ trials and CS− trials.
The shock epoch on reinforced CS+ (shocked) trials was modeled using the same temporal epoch for both non-reinforced CS+ and CS− trials.

The global mean signal level over all brain voxels was calculated for each time point and included to reduce the confounding effects of global signal change.

description.value: Twenty healthy participants (11 female) with mean age of 21.95 (range 18–35) participated in the study.

task_description.value: The conditioning task consisted of one run in which either the low- or high-pitched tone was paired with electric shock. A total of 30 trials were presented in a random order: 10 CS+ with shock, 10 CS+ without shock and 10 CS− tones. CS+ tones were followed by a shock with a 50% partial reinforcement schedule.

design_type.value: one run with trials presented in a random order

presentation_software.value: PsychToolbox extensions based on Matlab 2010b (MathWorks Corp., Natrick, MA, USA)

instructions.value: Participants were asked to indicate by button press with their index or middle finger of the right hand whether the tone was low or high pitched immediately after hearing the tone. Participants were informed of which CS would be paired with shock prior to study commencement.

stimuli.value: Two tones (500 and 1500 Hz) were adopted as conditioned stimuli (CSs). The mild electric shock used as an unconditioned stimulus (US) was delivered to the third and fourth fingers of the left hand.

task_performance_measures.value: low-versus-high-pitched tone discrimination by button press

task_description.value: The imaging session also involved a separate task following the conditioning phase; the details of this independent task were described previously by Lee et al. (2014).

description.value: High-resolution T1-MPRAGE structural images were acquired first.

modality.value: functional images with gradient-echo echo-planar T2*-weighted imaging

instrument.value: Siemens 3T Magnetom Trio with a 32-channel matrix head coil

description.value: Each functional volume consisted of 40 interleaved (no skip) 2.5 mm axial T2*-weighted slices. The images were acquired with a 64 × 64 matrix and a 192 mm field of view.

instrument.value: MP-150 system (BIOPAC System, Goleta, CA, USA), connected to a grounded RF filter, and MR-compatible leads and electrodes

description.value: Individual skin conductance responses were acquired with MRI-compatible electrodes placed on the index and middle finger of the left hand. All physiological data were recorded at 1 kHz sampling rates. SCR data were detrended and smoothed with a median filter over 50 samples to filter out MRI-induced noise. Due to a technical failure, recording could not be completed for one participant.

reason_no_modality_class_used.value: This was a physiological recording rather than MRI, EEG, fNIRS, or PET.

description.value: Standard preprocessing was conducted using FMRIBs Software Library (FSL), including slice-time correction, motion correction with MCFLIRT, spatial smoothing with a Gaussian kernel of full width at half maximum (FWHM) 6 mm, high-pass temporal filtering with a filter width of 100 s, skull stripping of structural images with FSL’s Brain Extraction Tool (BET), registration of each functional image to the participant’s high-resolution structural image and the standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) 2 mm brain, and removal of noise components with MELODIC ICA2. The first eight volumes were discarded to allow for signal equilibration.

model_settings.value: The model estimated individuals’ BOLD signal during the CS tone interval using regressors for non-reinforced CS+ trials and CS− trials. Six motion parameters and shock-reinforced trials were modeled as covariates of no interest. Group-level random-effects analysis was thresholded with a height threshold of Z > 2.3 and cluster corrected to p < 0.05 (one-tailed), using Gaussian Random Field Theory for whole-brain multiple-comparisons correction.

hrf_model.value: same temporal epoch for both non-reinforced CS+ and CS− trials

model_settings.value: The shock epoch on reinforced CS+ trials was modeled for 500 ms. Results were analyzed using anatomical ROIs of right and left S1.
The robust method identifies bivariate outliers and removes them in the calculation of a 95% confidence interval.

The analysis evaluated the total effect c, indirect path a, indirect path b, direct effect c’ after controlling for the indirect path, and mediation effect ab. The effect of A1 on right S1 activity was tested as mediated by amygdala reactivity.

A new design matrix contained unique trial-by-trial regressors for CS+ no shock and CS− trials, resulting in 20 independent variables (10 CS+ tones and 10 CS− tones). The global mean signal level over all brain voxels, motion parameters, and shock trials were included in the design matrix. Mean parameter estimates for each trial from the S1 seed region were correlated with signal from all other voxels, and correlation magnitudes were converted into z scores using the Fisher’s r-to-z transformation.
